entry.title: Shadow Warrior DC: 30th Anniversary Edition
entry.summary: The Dreamcast port of Shadow Warrior becomes the 30th Anniversary Edition: both official expansions built in, a new start-up screen, fewer disc reads during play and a new Performance Mode.
entry.content:
After what feels like a hundred more test builds... We're almost done!

It’s been a busy ten days for the Shadow Warrior Dreamcast port, now renamed 30th Anniversary Edition, because why the hell not.

The two official expansions, Twin Dragon and Wanton Destruction, are now fully integrated in the port, making it sort of a trilogy instead of a single game. Hence, "New Game" lists both original episodes alongside the two add-ons, and switching between them restarts quickly from a copy of the program kept in video RAM (as opposed to the original PC releases which actually had to completely reboot the game to load the expansions!). The menu picture stays on screen while it switches. "Load Game" has one save slot per game, and loading a save from another game switches to that game first.

The expansions also have their own credits pages, giving the original teams at Sunstorm Interactive, Level Infinity and Wylde Productions the credit they deserve (as far as I know, these credits were never there in the original PC releases). There is also a new start-up screen for the 30th anniversary, with one of four backgrounds picked at random each time you switch the console on!

Under the hood, most of the work went into smoother play. Art and sounds that used to be read from the disc mid-level are now loaded up front or streamed in the background. Free video RAM keeps a second copy of graphics, so the game reads from the disc much less often while you play. The renderer got several speed-ups, especially in Performance Mode (half-width 3D view), another new addition to this port.

Smaller touches: on-screen prompts now name the pad’s A and B buttons, and the test build shows a live FPS counter for testers. Next up is measuring every level on real hardware.

So... Who wants some Wang? 🥷

entry.title: Karnov MD: the simpler one?
entry.summary: Partly out of curiosity, partly because it looked easier to adapt than Tiger Road, and partly because an unofficial Neo Geo version exists, a few days ago I started porting Data East's Karnov to the Mega Drive. Here's where it stands.
entry.content:
Two weeks ago I started a new port: Data East's Karnov, from 1987, to the Mega Drive. In the arcade original you play Jinborov Karnovski, a fire-breathing Russian strongman who runs, jumps and climbs through nine stages, collecting items such as ladders, bombs, boomerangs and wings to get past each obstacle. Part of the motivation was knowing that an unofficial port of the arcade already exists for the Neo Geo, and part was thinking it would be less problematic to adapt than Tiger Road: fewer levels, fewer music tracks and, on the surface, a less advanced game. I may be wrong, as we'll see in future updates.

Like Tiger Road, the arcade board runs on a 68000, so this is another binary port: the original program runs on the Mega Drive, and a layer of glue code translates what it asks of the arcade hardware into Mega Drive graphics, palettes and sound. The differences are still there, though. The arcade shows 256×240 pixels and the Mega Drive 224 lines, so 8 lines are cropped from the top and 8 from the bottom. Its sound runs on a separate board with its own 6502 and two Yamaha FM chips (a YM2203 and a YM3526), so the music and effects are converted for a player of my own on the Mega Drive's Z80, using its FM and PSG channels, with a few effects played as the arcade's own samples through the DAC.

The first steps were analysis tools and a comparison of the different versions of the game, which ended with the Japanese one as the base. Within a few hours the port was booting to the title screen and playing the first stage with its scrolling background; then came the sprites and colours for each stage, the map screen between stages, a side-by-side comparison of all nine stages with the arcade, and finally the sound. Along the way, the coin-op leftovers went: no more INSERT COIN, no continues (game over takes you back to the title screen) and no FREE PLAY label in the demo. In their place there's a PRESS START prompt, a pause with its own PAUSE label, a difficulty selector on the title screen and a start-up notice with the build name.

The first builds had their share of bugs: black stripes on the background after dying, a GET READY message drawn in black, almost-black pieces left over the stage when switching to the map, half the frames going black during screen changes, music slowing down on the console whenever its Z80 was paused for DMA transfers, Karnov freezing at the start of a new stage, and pieces flickering on the map screen because too many sprites shared the same line. All of them are fixed now, and work continues on cutting dropped frames.

entry.title: Cruis'n USA DC: Arcade Edition
entry.summary: Almost there: the arcade Cruis'n USA running natively on the Dreamcast, now at full arcade speed on real hardware. Here's what it adds over the original.
entry.content:
Friendly reminder that Cruis'n USA: Arcade Edition is almost ready and I'm focusing now on tweaks, polishing and little performance optimizations.

As mentioned, this is not a port of the N64 release, nor does it emulate the arcade; instead, it translates the Midway V-Unit program from its released source code into native DC code and replaces its video and sound hardware with the Dreamcast's PowerVR and AICA.

Compared with the original arcade, naturally it adds Dreamcast controller support (analog stick or d-pad, triggers for gas and brake, and manual shifting on the d-pad), free play (no coins, no limited continues), pause with START during a race (the music keeps playing), high scores and settings saved to the VMU, the Midway logo on the VMU screen during attract mode, and controller vibration.

The hidden cars and tracks, which needed button combinations on the cabinet, are toggled with X and an on-screen prompt. Distant objects also fade in instead of popping up, and attract mode picks tracks at random (the original arcade would always feature the same demo tracks in the same order).

Over the last few weeks the work has focused on real hardware performance. Races now run at full arcade speed, and crashes into lamp posts, trees and cars still behave like the original even though the game moves further each frame. Iowa no longer reads from the CD nonstop (which was a problem during the first weeks of this project), several black screens have been fixed (after the high score table and when entering initials), and black lines and other artifacts have been virtually eradicated.

There is also a new "Arcade Edition" loading/logo screen with the build number, a GDEMU cover, and a number of rendering and code optimizations that make the game somewhat lighter.

Coming soon to a GitHub near you! You can follow me on X for more updates.

entry.title: Shadow Warrior DC: two weeks in
entry.summary: Two weeks of Shadow Warrior on the Dreamcast: fewer pauses for disc reads, saves that fit on a VMU, music that picks up where it left off, VGA output and a hand-drawn logo on the VMU.
entry.content:
Two weeks after the first post, the Dreamcast port has moved from "it runs" towards "it feels like a console game". Most of the work has gone into living with the console's limits: 16 MB of RAM, a CD drive instead of a hard disk, and a VMU with very little room for saves.

Some of the problems found along the way, and how they were solved:

  • Pauses to read the disc: any graphic or sound not already in memory meant stopping to read the CD in the middle of the action. Each level now preloads what fits in the cache by priority, leaving rare art for last, and makes sure Lo Wang's voice lines and pain grunts, explosion debris and the city's ambient sounds (sirens, traffic, aircraft, bikes) are always there. Diagnostic builds count every disc read during play to find what's still missing.
  • Music cut by data reads: the drive can't play a CD audio track and read data at the same time, so the music used to stop whenever the game loaded something. It now resumes from the point where it was cut instead of starting over.
  • Saves too big for a VMU: saves are now compressed in chunks straight to the file, store only what has changed since the level loaded, and use a half-size picture for the load menu. The settings file went down from 14 blocks to 5, and the game tells you how many blocks a save needs before writing it.
  • Speed: triple buffering, a larger 9 MB cache for the game's art, and faster code for drawing sprites, clearing the screen and copying memory.

And some additions for the Dreamcast version:

  • VGA output, for a sharper picture on a monitor.
  • A hand-drawn Shadow Warrior logo on the VMU screen outside play, in addition to the player's stats during the game.
  • The Options menu shows which controller slots are in use and the last jolt sent to the Jump Pack.
  • Menus moved and spaced so they fit within the visible area of a CRT, and calmer turning with the analog stick.
  • Shorter Credits screens with the port signed, keeping the original GPL notice scrolling underneath.

For more updates, you can follow me on X.

entry.title: Cruis'n USA DC: progress report
entry.summary: A few weeks into the Dreamcast port of the arcade Cruis'n USA: how the V-Unit code gets onto the console, the problems solved along the way, the extras, and where performance stands.
entry.content:
For a few weeks now I've been working on this Dreamcast port of the original arcade version of Cruis'n USA. As I mentioned before, this is not the N64 game, at all: it's the real arcade's graphics, sound, cars and tracks running natively on the DC. It's still a work in progress, but it already boots, plays full races and has been tested on real hardware through GDemu.

The arcade runs on Midway's V-Unit board, built around a TMS320C31 DSP and a custom polygon chip, so there's no ready-made path to the Dreamcast. The source code for the game was made public and I used it as a map, but rather than rewriting the game, the C31 machine code was first translated into C, which was then compiled for the Dreamcast's SH-4 with KallistiOS. The hottest routines (vertex transforms, polygon submission, object scanning) are rewritten by hand as native code. The V-Unit's polygon packets are converted on the fly into PowerVR polygons, and the DCS sound is pre-rendered into samples that play on the AICA. Everything is checked against a reference interpreter and against MAME, frame by frame where needed.

So yes, this was all a pain in the ass and turned out to be much more time-consuming than I initially thought, despite the source code being available, because the hardware used on the original arcade and the one inside our favourite white box are vastly different.

Some of the problems found along the way, and how they were solved:

  • Floating point: the C31 uses its own float format. Every value has to be converted to and from IEEE, thousands of times per frame. A bit-exact fast path, verified against all 4 billion possible values, gave a 6.6% speed-up on its own.
  • Memory: the translated code is several MB and the DC only has 16 MB of RAM. Most of it is compiled for size, with only the hot paths optimized for speed.
  • Timing: the game counts vertical blanks to move everything, and some animations advance once per game loop. The port follows a clock driven by the emulated C31 cycles, falling back to real time when the DC can't keep up, so menus run at the arcade's pace and races stay at the right speed.
  • Collisions: an addressing subtlety in the C31's parallel instructions scrambled every collision box. Cars hit you without touching and fences were ignored. Collision rates now match MAME. This is still the port's main weak point, though.
  • Real PowerVR vs emulators: issues that Flycast and Redream don't show (stray lines on distant cars, polygon list overflows) were tracked down with diagnostic builds on real consoles. Still needs fixes, though.
  • Textures: the arcade's 8-bit paletted texture pages are converted to ARGB1555 and cached in VRAM, with large textures stored at half resolution to fit.

On the other hand, some extras for this port are:

  • No RAM/ROM check or Midway/Nintendo weird-looking loading screen: new, cleaner, faster custom loading screen with the game's logo.
  • VMU saves and logo, Jump Pack support.
  • A fade-in for objects popping up on the horizon. The original was far from perfect in the drawing distance / popping department, so this is me trying to hide or partially solve that.
  • And all the arcade's hidden cars and tracks, unlockable from their menus with the X button.

Current status: races run mostly at 28.5 fps, the same rate as the arcade, with drops to 19 fps in the busiest scenes. The attract demo is still heavier, and performance work continues. Feedback from people testing on real hardware has been invaluable so far, so comments and testing reports are very welcome.

More news soon!

entry.title: Cruis'n USA DC: the arcade, not the N64
entry.summary: Bringing the original arcade Cruis'n USA to the Dreamcast, starting from the arcade code rather than the Nintendo 64 version, and finding out the hardware gap is wider than I thought.
entry.content:
This is not a port of the Nintendo 64 version of Cruis'n USA. The starting point is the original arcade code, the program that ran on Midway's V-Unit hardware, which has been made public. The idea is to bring the arcade game itself to the Dreamcast, with its own graphics, sound and handling, rather than adapt the home conversion.

I naively thought it would be simpler than it is. The arcade's main processor is a Texas Instruments TMS320C31, a DSP that has nothing in common with the Dreamcast's SH-4, so its code can't just run: it first ran through an interpreter, and then through a static recompiler that translates the C31 code into C, checked against the interpreter so both behave the same. The 3D is just as different. The arcade prepares its scenes for its own polygon hardware, so the routines that transform vertices and send polygons have to be rewritten natively for the PowerVR, and the textures converted on the fly. Sound comes from a separate DCS board; for now, the game's sounds are pre-rendered with MAME into a sound bank that the Dreamcast plays back following the same DCS commands the game sends.

Four days in, it boots on the console and runs races with sound, saves the arcade's settings to the VMU (whose screen also shows your position and speed), supports the Jump Pack, and is being tested on real hardware, which has already turned up its own set of hangs and glitches. The big fight ahead is speed: getting a frame rate that feels like the arcade.

entry.title: Shadow Warrior DC: the console version it never had
entry.summary: A fan port of 3D Realms' 1997 Build engine shooter to the Dreamcast, starting from the released source code and its portable JFShadowWarrior version.
entry.content:
Shadow Warrior came out in 1997, made by 3D Realms, the same people behind Duke Nukem 3D, and running on the same engine, Ken Silverman's Build. Unlike Duke, it never made it to the consoles of its day: there was no version for the PlayStation or the Saturn, nor later for the Dreamcast or the PS2. This is a fan port to put that right, at least on the Dreamcast.

The starting point is the original code, released by 3D Realms under the GPL in 2005, or more precisely the portable version of it published as JFShadowWarrior (JFSW), which already runs on modern systems. On top of that goes a Dreamcast layer built on KallistiOS: graphics, sound effects through the console's AICA sound chip, music as CD audio tracks, and support for the controller, keyboard and VMU. Build draws everything in software, so it's the Dreamcast's SH-4 that renders every frame, and the PowerVR only has to put it on screen. The several screen resolutions the original code offered have been removed, leaving the game at a fixed 320×240, and so have some of the more exotic features the Dreamcast port would never use anyway, such as voxels.

The first playable build came together within a few hours of starting. A few days in, settings and saved games live on the VMU, compressed so a save fits in its few blocks; the VMU screen shows the title and the player's stats; the Jump Pack rumbles on hits, heavy weapons and earthquakes; and an Options menu lets you switch on the PC cheat codes from the pad. Real hardware is already proving stricter than the emulators, with crashes from memory reads the SH-4 won't tolerate.

entry.title: Tiger Road NG: day one
entry.summary: A second Tiger Road port, this time to the Neo Geo: the same arcade code, with backgrounds rebuilt from sprites and the music adapted to a different sound chip.
entry.content:
Practically at the same time as the Mega Drive port, I started a second one, this time to the Neo Geo. SNK's hardware also pairs a 68000 with a Z80 for sound, so the same binary-port approach applies, and much of the groundwork from the Mega Drive version (tools, documentation, notes on the arcade code) could be reused from the start.

The big difference is video: the Neo Geo has no tile-based background layers, only sprites and a fixed text layer, so the arcade's scrolling backgrounds have to be rebuilt out of sprites. Within a few hours the original program was booting through to the title screen and the attract demo, with the arcade's colours mapped to the Neo Geo palette and the picture matching the arcade. Unlike the Mega Drive, though, the Neo Geo has no 256-pixel-wide mode: its screen is 320 pixels wide, so for now, until I find an alternative (if there is one), the game runs with black bars on both sides.

Sound took a different path. The arcade's original Z80 program runs on the Neo Geo's own Z80, with a driver that translates its output for the YM2610. The catch is that the arcade board has two YM2203 chips, six FM channels in total, while the YM2610 only has four, and squeezing the music into four channels meant losing parts of it, the bass among them. The answer was a mixed approach: some parts of the arcade music recorded as ADPCM-B samples and triggered in time with the rest. And since the port is meant for both MVS cabinets and AES home consoles, those first days also covered coins and DIP switches for the former, and free play with a difficulty menu for the latter.

entry.title: Tiger Road MD: day one
entry.summary: Starting a Mega Drive port of Capcom's Tiger Road by running the arcade's own 68000 code on the console.
entry.content:
Tiger Road (Tora-he no Michi) is a 1987 action platformer by Capcom. It was released between Ghosts'n Goblins (1985) and Ghouls'n Ghosts (1988) and shares their style of platforming and gameplay, but set in medieval China.

The project is to port it to several classic consoles, starting with the Mega Drive, which will naturally be the one that takes a few cuts (at least until someone with a lot more talent does it better).

It runs on a "Capcom-based" or pre-CPS board, and its CPU and sound chips are reasonably similar to the Mega Drive's. Its resolution is 256×224, which matches one of the console's video modes, meaning it fills the screen with nothing lost and no need to crop or stretch the graphics.

So instead of rewriting the game the plan is a binary port: the original 68000 code runs on the console, and a layer of glue code translates what it asks of the arcade hardware into Mega Drive graphics, palettes and sound. The first hours went into rebuilding the ROM, extracting the graphics, taking measurements in MAME and putting together a test ROM to find out whether the idea was viable at all.

A couple days later the first level scrolled with its sprites, the arcade's colours had been squeezed into the Mega Drive's four 16-colour palettes, the music and effects were running on the arcade's original Z80 program, and graphics were being sent by DMA straight from ROM to save CPU time. Testing on real hardware through a flashcart brought its own round of fixes, starting with keeping DMA transfers within what fits in vertical blank. The goal from here is a playable ROM that stays as faithful to the arcade as possible, accepting some cuts in colour and sound along the way.

Everything is being done from the original arcade ROM. Apart from personal taste, I chose this game because, as far as I know, it doesn't step on any other homebrew project already under way. I'm doing all this for fun, and to learn with the tools I now have at hand, mostly through my work.

Once I'd confirmed it could be done, I started adapting it in parallel to the Neo Geo, Saturn and Dreamcast.
